justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across all three horizons, starting near 97.5 for the one-day forecast and rising gradually to 99.5 at one month. This pattern assumes mean-reversion tendencies are relatively weak and that whatever underlying trend or momentum existed at the time of the forecast would persist mildly into the future. The one-day estimate is anchored most heavily to the last observed value, with only a small adjustment for any directional signal present in recent price action or fundamental indicators. As the horizon extends to one week and one month, I incorporated a slight positive drift assumption, reflecting a long-run tendency for the asset or index in question to trend upward over time, though the magnitude of that drift is modest relative to the uncertainty involved.

The confidence interval widths expand substantially as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 5.4 units, capturing intraday and overnight volatility that is relatively well-characterized by recent historical data. By one week, the interval widens to 11 units, incorporating the possibility of multi-day momentum swings, macro data releases, or sentiment shifts. At one month, the interval broadens to 23 units, reflecting the much larger set of possible paths the asset could take, including trending, mean-reverting, or choppy behavior across dozens of trading sessions.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden macro shock — such as an unexpected central bank policy shift, a geopolitical escalation, or a significant credit event — could produce a sharp selloff that breaks below the lower bound of even the one-month interval. Liquidity crises or correlated asset unwinds can cause moves that exceed what historical volatility distributions would predict. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst such as better-than-expected economic data, a policy pivot, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical tension could drive the asset significantly above my upper bounds.

It is also worth noting that my intervals are calibrated around a roughly normal distribution of outcomes, which likely underweights fat-tail events. Real financial markets exhibit excess kurtosis, meaning extreme moves happen more frequently than a Gaussian model would suggest. If volatility itself shifts — for example, if implied volatility spikes due to an options-driven event or a macro uncertainty regime change — then the realized distribution of outcomes over the next month could look quite different from what my confidence intervals imply. These structural limitations are a standing caveat on any probabilistic forecast of this type.
